title: ASIC targets risky trading
full_text:
Australia’s corporate cop wants to extend its crackdown on high-risk financial products, proposing that restrictions aimed at curbing investor losses remain in place for at least another decade.
The Australian Securities & Investments Commission said on Monday it wants to retain the product intervention order on contracts-for-difference for a further 10 years and broaden its scope.
CFDs are complex, leveraged, high-risk bets on whether the price of an asset will go up or down. The current product intervention order, in place since 2021, limits the leverage retail investors can use and provides protections that reduce the scale and speed of potential losses.
ASIC has previously warned that leverage and associated financing fees can magnify investor losses on these over-the-counter products.
“The evidence demonstrates that ASIC’s CFD intervention order has materially reduced retail investor harm by addressing key drivers of harm, like excess leverage,” ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said. “Within six months of our current order taking effect, aggregate net losses by retail client accounts fell by 91 per cent.” ASIC also wants to amend the intervention order so that CFDs settled through digital assets are captured alongside those settled by cash or so-called ‘set-off’, which is done by netting out profits and losses.
“These proposals seek to make the investing landscape safer by ensuring our consumer protection measures keep pace as financial markets continue to evolve,” Mr Kirkland said.
“Some products expose retail investors to the same risks as CFDs but may fall outside the current PIO because of how they are settled.
“The proposed updates ensure protections apply consistently, regardless of whether a CFD is settled by cash, set-off or digital assets,” he said.
The regulator, which is also mulling a retail investor ban on CFDs over options, has given the industry four weeks to have its say on the proposals. ASIC’s renewed push against risky CFDs comes after the regulator earlier this year forced CFD operators to refund nearly $40m to retail investors after finding the sector was flouting the product intervention order.
More than half of CFD issuers in the market had contravened the order by offering ‘margin discounts’ to retail clients who took on opposing long and short positions, ASIC found. These investors incurred higher funding costs but could not profit from their opposing CFD positions, the regulator said. ASIC also raised concerns about misleading marketing and lack of monitoring by issuers.
